A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same APEX research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval, docking-score enrichment, regression, runtime, and Thompson-sampling comparison results on its constructed combinatorial libraries.

after.justification: v2 retains original BRICS-library experiments and reports additional Enamine REAL evaluations, error analyses, budget-dependent retrieval results, and counter-screening experiments.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same noisy-embedding surrogate, frozen-embedding reconstruction by the hierarchical factorizer, additive synthon contributions, and GPU top-k procedure. The reformulated loss notation and newly disclosed architecture details do not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot evaluation on the commercial Enamine REAL 70B library, extending beyond v1's constructed BRICS libraries. Figure 2 additionally evaluates Wager CNS constraints, and Appendix A.11 introduces selective counter-screening and a composite five-target objective. The original five protein targets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Thompson sampling and random/background comparisons remain. Figure 10 newly compares the unfactorized surrogate against APEX on retrieval across evaluation budgets; v1 compared these models only on endpoint regression accuracy. The numerous methods added to related work are not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include zero-shot transfer with a 100,000-compound Enamine background sample, recall sweeps across evaluation budgets, and Kendall's tau-b and Spearman's rho metrics. Counter-screening imposes median-score thresholds on four non-objective targets and evaluates 100 compounds after true-objective reranking. These substantially expand evaluation design; Appendix A.8's training details are disclosures, not established changes to prior settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds endpoint-wise surrogate/factorizer error decomposition, retrieval sensitivity to evaluation budget, and comparisons diagnosing the effect of factorization on recall. Zero-shot Enamine evaluation tests transfer across libraries, while Appendix A.11 examines selectivity and composite-objective behavior. These analyses go substantially beyond v1's regression and retrieval comparisons.

E5.justification: Figure 2C newly reports mean recall and standard deviation across the five targets. This quantifies between-target variation, not uncertainty across independent training runs. Table 1 retains averaging over five objective-specific runs; no increase in repeated runs or seeds is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds Enamine accuracy, enrichment, and runtime results, plus Wager CNS, budget-sweep, error-decomposition, and counter-screening outcomes. Table 1 retains the BRICS timings and adds, for example, 202.4 seconds for GPU retrieval of one million Lipinski-constrained compounds from REAL 70B. Existing regression values also change: surrogate R-squared for n_unspecified_stereocenter is approximately 0.61 in v1 Figure 7 versus 0.04 in v2 Figure 6, without an explanation of the revision.

T1.justification: Appendix A.6 adds the prediction-error and expected-MSE decompositions in Equations 24–25, including the cross term and the approximation when it is negligible. Appendix A.1 adds an asymptotic encoder-cost claim. The original optimization and factorization mathematics remains substantively unchanged; these are limited theoretical additions.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims about fast exhaustive approximate retrieval, constraint handling, and the benchmark contribution. Section 2 newly makes an explicit priority claim that APEX is the first application of factorization-based retrieval to virtual screening of combinatorial synthesis libraries.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the error decomposition as indicating largely independent error sources and identifies which component should be improved for different endpoints. It also discusses MET's weaker zero-shot transfer and possible fine-tuning, and explains the selectivity-versus-absolute-score tradeoff in counter-screening. These add substantial diagnostic interpretation absent from v1.

D1.justification: Appendix A.8 newly specifies MPNN layers, pooling, dimensions, parameter counts, Adam optimization, learning rate, iteration limit, the 80/20 surrogate split, and factorizer fine-tuning. Appendix A.3 and Table 2 document the existing 28 endpoints and their computation. These substantially improve implementation disclosure; the code, data, and weights pointers remain substantively unchanged.

R1.justification: A dedicated Related Work section substantially expands v1's brief positioning. It discusses surrogate and active-learning screening, protein–ligand representation methods such as ConPLex and DrugCLIP, synthesizable generative models, and factorization precedents. It newly articulates complementarity with representation-learning methods and explicit factorization-based novelty.

P1.justification: The abstract, core data/method exposition, and conclusion are largely retained. Editorial changes concentrate on the introduction and Thompson-sampling explanation, insertion of dedicated related work, separation of enrichment and runtime discussions, and organization of the expanded appendix. Venue, affiliation, and disclosure text also changes.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from a single-column to a two-column layout, relocates the library-construction and enrichment figures to the appendix, and substantially reorganizes the recall and regression displays. It expands the runtime table, adds an endpoint-description table, and introduces error-decomposition, budget-sweep, and counter-screening figures.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses two important weaknesses of v1: validation confined to constructed BRICS libraries and sparse architecture/training documentation. Commercial-library zero-shot results strengthen evidence of applicability, while Appendix A.8 improves reproducibility and the new diagnostics clarify error sources and screening tradeoffs. These gains outweigh localized theoretical overstatement, notably Appendix A.1's unsupported characterization of encoding cost as logarithmic in library size.
